content.summary_of_the_paper:
The problem of causal inference in the case where timeseries data is to be analyzed is tackled.
In particular, the author/s start/s from observing that the existing literature lacks in taking into proper account the duration of events and thus current approaches and algortihms fail to properly assess causal reletionships between events when ignoring the duration of events preceding the target event. 
The paper states to make four contributions:
- a new causal model to analyze event data by properly exploiting duratin of events is presented
- a set of causal event scores to be used to assess causability between events
- a set of numerical experiments based on synthetic data and two real world datasets which are often used in the specialized literature
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength
- the problem analyzed is extremely relvant and has many real world applications in healtcare, medicine, finance, ...
- numerical experiments partially support the proposed approach

Weaknesses
- the paper is not easy to read, its' structure, writing style and notations are difficult to follow for the interested reader, the reader interested to appreciate the contributions of the paper.
- the notation is cumbersome and complex to help the interested reader to follow the paper arguments, furthermore some definitions clash to each other, terms used to represent a quantity are then later on used to represent completely different quantities.

- Granger causality has little to do with causality, therefore if the paper is about causality I would expect to read clearly which are the assumptions to ensure what is discovered is a causal reletionship instead of a purly associational one.

- lacking literature, many papers are missing in the discussion about literature, please check Universal Models of Multivariate Temporal Point Processes, Asela Gunawardana, Chris Meek. Proceedings of the 19th International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics, PMLR 51:556-563, 2016 (and connected literature)

- contibutions are truly marginal and incremental, the paper extends an existing method to cope with durations of events. Furthermore, I beg to disagree with this definition of duration because you are considering discrete time intervals. Indeed, you do not cope with durations or at least you do not coform to the definition of events duration which must be continuous and not discrete.

- extremely critical to make the decision about the lenght of each interval, changing the lenght you inevitably will end up with completely different model for predicting events, this aspect is completely verloked while it is of paramount relevance

- In formula (1), I kindly ask the author/s to discuss which values the D's ratio can take, 

- Theorem 1, mentions dependence while in previous part of the paper you mentioned causal relationship, can you please clarify?

- Formula (7) maybe better to use a different notation other than D wich has been already used, I know you write that now it has  different meaning but this makes the interested reader to be continuously confused

- I do not know what an indication function is while I know about indicator function

- just below formula (8) you use t to represent time while according to your notation before t was intended to represent intervals. However, it may be the case I'm wrong

- results of numerical experiemnts only partially support the effectiveness of the proposed score and framework

- in related works I read "contemporaneous causality", I miss what you mean by this, would you be that kind to help me understand?

- what does it happen when you observe many event types? what happens when many events appear and disappear in the temporal sequence? Which the lenght of the time interval?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is difficult to read and follow, its structure, writing and notation make not easy, in my humble opinion, for the genuinely interested reader to gain understanding of what developed and proposed by the paper.
The quality is limited, because in my humble opinion the contributions of the paper are marginal and incermental with respect to existing literature, even if the idea to take into account duration is at the same time relevant and not truly new.
Therefore, also the novelty is limited while reproducibility is somewhat potentially ensured by the available links of the paper.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The paper tackles a very important problem, with many real world applications.
However, it fails to make a sensible contibution to the specialized literature, this motivated by all wecknesses I listed above which are major criticisms to what described in the paper.
Therefore, I recommend rejection of the paper.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a causal inference method between events based on historical counts combined with a time window. The authors claim that existing point process models are too limited because they either assume regular time intervals or use a parametric model.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths

- Formalized an easy-to-apply method for causal discovery. 

Weakness

- The underlying probabilistic model is not clearly defined. Apparently, the random variables are binary, with 1 observing an event within the window and 0 otherwise. 

- The novelty of the work is not very clear. The ratio of the occurrence count to the duration is typically called the event rate, which is the basis of the most basic stochastic processes. It is not clear what novelty was added to those existing models. 

- There seem to be many related works that are not discussed in this paper. For example, association-rule-based approaches have been applied to a similar task for years such as the below. The authors could have discussed the novelty of the proposed approach in light of those studies. The authors are also encouraged to discuss computational cost. 
 
> Li, J., Le, T. D., Liu, L., Liu, J., Jin, Z., & Sun, B. (2013, December). Mining causal association rules. In 2013 IEEE 13th International Conference on Data Mining Workshops (pp. 114-123). IEEE.

> Tung, Anthony K. H., et al. "Efficient mining of inter transaction association rules." IEEE transactions on Knowledge and Data Engineering 15.1 (2003): 43-56.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The text is mostly well-written. However, discussions on some of the related works seem missing, making the overall contribution a bit unclear.
content.summary_of_the_review: It is not clear what kind of methodological contribution has been made by the paper. I encourage the authors to explore a specific application, in which the proposed approach works much better than the alternatives. As I mentioned above, similar approaches may have been used within, e.g., the association rule mining framework, which seems to use similar settings (windows, supports, time-order, etc.). The paper would be much stronger if the paper could make a clear case against those existing works.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper introduces a method of finding causal relationships within time series (called here temporal events) while including the duration of said events into the model. The paper follows the previous work of Bhattacharjya et al. (2021) very closely. In particular, the authors define "necessity" and "sufficiency causality" (which are probabilistic measures of temporal alignment of events) and the "Duration-based Necessity-Sufficiency Trade-off Score" (DNST), which combines the two. Subsequently, they show that DNST measures the dependence of temporal events. As the next step, the "Duration-based Conditional Intensity Rate Causality Score" (DCIR), a relaxation of DNST, is introduced along with its "multi-cause" extension. The authors show that DCIR, again, measures independence of temporal events, while the multi-cause DCIR measures conditional independence. The paper concludes with a synthetic and real-world experiment that compares the proposed approach (DNST and DCIR scores) to the baseline of Bhattacharjya et al. (2021) on the Hits@k measure showing the the current approach beats the baseline.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
STRENGTHS

The paper introduces one novel idea, that is the incorporation of event duration to the modelling of temporal causal relationships. The experiments suggest that this incorporation indeed boosts the performance of temporal-causal relationships recovery.


WEAKNESSES

The main weakness of the paper is its limited novelty. The event duration is added to the definitions in a straightforward way (such as Eq. (1) and (4)), but the remainder of the results (theorems) as well as the structure of the entire paper mirrors Bhattacharjya et al. (2021), the only difference being the rather simple adjustment for event duration.

The limited novelty might not be detrimental to the paper if the authors  focused more on the interpretation of event duration in their model (since it is the only thing that differentiates it from previous work). There is no discussion on what the causal meaning of event duration is and how its incorporation translates to better results. What causal phenomena are captured by the event duration? Is the set of potential confounders smaller for longer events? Does the model capture co-occurring events more easily? How exactly does the model behavior change when we "switch off" modelling the event duration (such an ablation study might be a good motivation for the entire approach)?

The addition of event duration also begs the question of whether instantaneous coupling (or overlapping) of events can be modeled as well. Perhaps this is the reason the model works better with event duration?

A minor issue is that some "causal" claims are not clear (or at least, the terms used are not defined): e.g. Section 1, Contributions: "We prove that the proposed duration-based scores follow the causality hypothesis testing framework." What is this framework? Does it mean that the measures used correspond to conditional independence testing? This is a very general feature of causal models and I am not sure how to interpret such proof as contribution.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is clear, well-written and easy to follow. The originality is somewhat limited (see above).
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper introduces a minor extension (the incorporation of event duration) to an existing approach (Bhattacharjya et al. (2021)). All the theoretical results are straightforward extensions of Bhattacharjya et al. (2021) as well. The authors also do not use the opportunity to elaborate on the causal meaning of the duration or why it leads to slightly better results than those from Bhattacharjya et al. (2021). I think that, given limited novelty of the approach, a thorough discussion of the mechanism in which the model is able to use event duration would make the paper much more interesting.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a method for inferring causal dependence between temporal events that takes into account even duration. The paper proposes a set of duration-based event causality (DEC) scores and shows empirically that those score aid causal inference.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
\+ The paper is well-written and clear.

– The author's framework introduces a great deal of additional complexity into causal inference. This is not necessarily a bad thing, but it does introduce a set of extra complexities, some of which include: (1) Rather than a single value for an event, there can how be an entire profile of values over time for the event (e.g., rain intensity)?; (2) Does the occurrence of an event cause another event, or does the value profile of that event matter in terms of causing another event?; (3) What influences the duration between events?; (4) Does the duration or value profile of one event help determine the duration or value profile of another event?; (5) Does the gap between events affect the duration or value profile?

– The empirical evaluation (Section 4) appears to be entirely associational rather than causal. That is, the evaluation determines whether the proposed measures provide better "Hits@K" (an associational measure) rather than whether the effect of interventions are correctly inferred. The latter is difficult (Dorie et al. 2019; Gentzel et al 2019), but not impossible. Note also that finding associations can still be interesting, but the paper claims that the goals is causal inference.

– The current version of the paper has a minor but annoying problem with citations. Specifically, citations that should show up in parentheses do not, and this can make reading occasionally difficult. For example: "There has been extensive research focusing on learning Granger causality in temporal data, e.g., based on graphical models Lozano et al. (2009), Peters et al. (2013) and Hawkes processes Achab et al. (2017)."

References

Dorie, V., Hill, J., Shalit, U., Scott, M., & Cervone, D. (2019). Automated versus do-it-yourself methods for causal inference: Lessons learned from a data analysis competition. Statistical Science, 34(1), 43-68.

Gentzel, A., Garant, D., & Jensen, D. (2019). The case for evaluating causal models using interventional measures and empirical data. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 32.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Overall, clarity, quality, novelty, and reproducibility all appear good.

To slightly improve clarity, the authors may want to describe casual graphical models as being concerned with instantaneous events with no information about time ordering. In contrast, the authors assume that events are not instantaneous and that they have time ordering information.
content.summary_of_the_review: The authors propose measures intended to aid discovery of causal dependencies in event data.  However, the empirical evaluation in the paper appears to be entirely associational. Thus, the empirical evaluation provides little support for the claims of the authors in the first section of the paper.
